detail: The purple guild is a religious college based on Cyprus (Alashiya). Its own cult is rooted in the Minoan goddess, and it is bound to no single kingdom's priesthood, Egyptian or otherwise. It no longer reveres Knossos and keeps no pilgrimage rights or caretakers in the ruins where the Sherden train. Its name will be a Minoan-derived title and is not yet chosen.

The guild holds the only working method for turning raw murex secretion into the draw. It does all processing itself and none of it on the mainland, obtaining the raw material from Tyre through trade. It works in lamplit, windowless vault-workshops, seals the liquor in closed jars, and stores the draw dried to powder in the dark. This overrides the earlier proposals of a Tyrian royal dark-workshop and of the catch being split on Tyre's shore.

The potency lies in the gland secretion before light touches it. The guild's 'purple' is the nearly colourless, unsunned draw. Sunlight does not destroy the potency; it changes it. A dose for drinking is graded by how little light the draw has seen. Weapon- and armour-working uses the raw precursor, not the finished dye. The recreational low-dose psychedelic is the sunned dregs, nearly spent.

Tyre controls the purple supply through the murex beds off its coast, worked by divers and trap-setters with baited wicker traps on floats, the snails kept alive in seawater pools. Tyre's dominance over northern Canaan rests on this access. Its daylight dye yards make the dye it sells. The dependence is mutual: the guild needs Tyre's beds, and Tyre cannot make nodes. Tyre's royal house knows the supply is its strongest lever over the guild and resents the guild for making what Tyre cannot.
Assyria's raids on northern Canaan are partly aimed at Tyre's dye coast, where the purple supply comes from.

Candidates enter the guild in youth from good families, which compete for places as they do for the House of Life. Formation is a 10–14 year ladder of rising doses and House-of-Life style training (hieratic, Akkadian, the guild's script and protocols) with formal examinations between stages. Rank names are placeholders. A novice entering at 16–18 becomes a node at about 28–32, and no child ever links. The ladder ends in a final, dangerous dose: some do not survive it and others come out unable to link. Those who fail keep their standing and become guild archivists, envoys, temple scribes or provincial voices. This replaces magic.md's 'takes children young and feeds them purple until they gain powers'.

Nodes are mature, highly educated adults: diplomats and archivists as much as relays. They are celibate, give up their family name at the final dose, and are bound to the guild for life by the high dose. A node can link to every other node and only to nodes, a lifelong tether that can never be fully switched off. The cost is erasure of self, not madness, and nodes are permanently 'a little elsewhere'. They wear purple-striped robes, among the few non-royals entitled to purple. They are housed in temples or palaces, and senior nodes sit at court beside the high priests.

The guild swears to carry every message for every paying crown and never to reveal one. The oath is truly kept: not even the record of who wrote to whom is sold. A node who reveals a message is put to death by the guild itself. Relay is word for word, and a node who alters a message disgraces the whole college. Unlike ordinary envoys, nodes are never detained or harmed, because every court needs them. Kings pay heavily to keep a node at court. Nodes are very valuable.
The guild serves whoever holds Egypt's throne. After the coup it serves Pentawer.

The conspirators use the guild's network. In the same season the guild carries their traffic and Ramesses III's own messages and warns no one. Its stance afterward is 'We carried; we do not judge.' When Ramesses III dies, the Pi-Ramesses node relays the news, and Isis and the Assyrian court both learn of it through the guild. After the coup, the guild's supply runs through a Tyre at war with Egypt's new ally, Assyria.

The pleasure trade in sunned dregs is a black market. The cheap stuff is weak, the strong stuff rare, and a bad batch dangerous. The guild sees recreational use as a profanation of its sacrament and keeps account of who has profaned it.
Aegon's party purple is the black-market sunned dregs. He is high on them the night his protector dies; the death is not necessarily an overdose. Years of abuse leave him scarred.

A guild node is posted at the court of Pi-Ramesses: a highborn adult who spent their youth on the ladder, respected, wealthy and permanently a little elsewhere. The conspirators must either time the killing around this node's duties or count on the guild's neutrality.

It is a religious college with its own cult rooted in the Minoan goddess, independent of any kingdom's priesthood, including Egypt's. It is based on Cyprus (Alashiya). Its name will be a Minoan-derived title and has not yet been chosen.

Cyprus is the purple guild's base. The college moved there after Knossos fell because the island already had murex works and copper wealth and stands between the great powers. All processing of the draw happens there, under the guild.

Minoan palace priestesses on Crete (Keftiu) discovered it around 1800 BCE by drinking the unripened gland liquor as a visionary sacrament. The power to communicate across distance emerged generations later among the oldest, lifelong-dosed priestesses. Tyre's Melqart's-dog myth is a later civic claim. Tyre controls the raw supply through its murex beds, and its rise rests on that, but only the guild can process the draw.
How many candidates wash out of the ladder or die at the final dose, as a proportion of those who enter?
What is the guild's Minoan-derived name?
What are the final names of the ranks: Novice/Listener/Regency/Voice/Node, or Candidate/Adept/Node?
If only nodes can link, how do Listeners, Regency and Voices practise relay?
How far does a node's link reach?
How is entry decided: hereditary houses, sponsorship, aptitude testing, or a mix?
Do royal younger children ever enter the guild?
In what form does the raw material cross from Tyre to the guild: live snails, cut glands, or something else?
Which murex species is the guild's prize?
Do the shades of the draw correspond to different powers, or only to different strengths?
Does fully ripened dye on finished cloth have any effect on dyers or wearers?
Where do the recreational dregs leak from, and who runs the black market?
Does the guild formally ban recreational use, or only scorn it?
Who supplies the precursor for weapon-working, and does the guild control that trade?
Do the Sherden super-soldier injections, if real, draw on the draw, and does the guild know?
Did the purple priesthood know about or work with Knossos's griffin-keepers?
Is the guild's neutrality real, or does it quietly favour whoever protects Cyprus?
Can a king have a node recalled or replaced?
Do nodes retire, and what remains of them?
Is the Senior Node the node posted at Pi-Ramesses, or someone else?
How many nodes exist, and which courts hold one?
The founding legend. Two long-dosed Minoan priestesses first hear each other across the sea, between Knossos and the Chrysi dye-beds.
A forgotten shrine. The guild has abandoned Knossos, but an oldest shrine of the purple cult could lie sealed in the ruins for Jon to stumble on.
News reaches Jon first. A node relays the coup to Crete long before any ship could, and Jon hears his father is dead from a stranger's mouth.
The Assyrian channel. The guild may be the channel through which the Assyrian marriage was negotiated before the coup, carried word for word and never revealed.
"We carried; we do not judge." Isis or Jon learns the guild carried the conspiracy. Isis pushes Tyre to squeeze the supply in punishment, even if that blinds her own children's allies.
Tiye's weapon. Tiye sends her orders through the guild precisely because she knows its fidelity means it will not interfere.
Executing its own. The guild executes one of its own for revealing a message, and the audience at court sees the oath's price.
Breaking the monopoly. The guild secretly seeds beds on Cyprus or in Crete's old dye coves, a silkworm-theft move that could end Tyre's hold.
The cutoff clock. An Assyrian raid on the dye coast puts a countdown on how long the guild's stored draw lasts.
A death at the final dose. Someone tied to a main character dies at the final dose, revealing the toll behind the guild's prestige.
